abstract: This paper describes the current arrangements for the procurement of ancillary services and how these services may be procured under NETA. The paper is separated into five sections. The first section outlines the categories of ancillary services that currently exist, the current procurement procedures. The second section outlines recent developments. Section three briefly describes the new market arrangements. Section four summarises Ofgem's views on the procurement of ancillary services under NETA as set out in the recent consultation. Finally, section five outlines the authors' views on the procurement of ancillary services in the future.

abstract: The new energy trading arrangements (NETA) should focus electricity suppliers and customers alike on the value of load management which, for the purposes of this paper, is defined as actual demand being as close as a possible to forecast demand for any given period. Large suppliers will be able to manage their risk effectively through large-scale aggregation and so little may appear to change. However smaller niche supply companies, who may be focusing on strategic large consumers, will look for tools to help them efficiently manage their demand portfolio.

abstract: The author describes how the implementation of a wide range of load management initiatives helped Ireland's Electricity Supply Board (ESB) cope with a growth of almost 50% between 1991 and 1999. ESB will continue to promote the efficient use of electricity through the delivery of value added services to customers. He argues, however, that it is important that all the new players entering the new electricity industry in 2000 should also be involved in a co-ordinated approach to deliver national load management objectives and, possibly, national environmental objectives.

articleTitle: The reasons behind the new electricity trading arrangements
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Electricity Trading (Ref. No. 2000/038)
abstract: Ten years ago, almost exactly, the UK electricity industry moved from public ownership and into private hands. The change brought market cultures to an industry that had grown to maturity in the ownership of the State. Here, the author describes how, in the period since that major transition the industry has undergone more major changes-substantial restructuring, the progressive introduction of supply competition and significant new entry into the generation market-driven by the needs of competition.
